O(2n)
O(n²)
O(log n)
questions.explanation: The inner loop runs n times for each of the n passes of the outer loop, so `count += 1` runs n × n times: O(n²). O(2n) would describe two loops one *after* the other (and simplifies to O(n)); nested loops multiply, they do not add.

questions.stem: Which line orders these growth rates from slowest-growing (best) to fastest-growing (worst) for large n?
options: O(1) < O(n) < O(log n) < O(n log n) < O(2ⁿ) < O(n²)
O(1) < O(log n) < O(n log n) < O(n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ)
O(log n) < O(1) < O(n) < O(n²) < O(n log n) < O(2ⁿ)
O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ)
questions.explanation: Constant does not grow at all; log n grows very slowly (about 20 for a million items); then n; then n log n, which is n multiplied by a growing factor and so is *larger* than n; then n²; and 2ⁿ, which doubles with every extra item and overtakes any power of n. Putting n log n before n is the usual slip.

options: O(n²), because there are two loops
O(n), because the two loops run one after the other
O(log n), because each loop does very little work
O(1), because it only returns two numbers
questions.explanation: Each loop visits the n items once, so the total is n + n = 2n steps, which is O(n). Loops only multiply when one is *inside* the other; here they run in sequence, so they add.

questions.stem:
What is the time complexity (tightest Big-O) of `steps(n)`?

```python
def steps(n):
    count = 0
    while n > 1:
        n = n // 2
        count += 1
    return count
```
options: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(log n)
questions.explanation: n is halved on every iteration, so the number of iterations is about log₂ n: 64 needs 6 halvings, and doubling n to 128 adds only one more. O(n) would need n to go down by a fixed amount each time (n - 1, n - 2, ...), not by half.

questions.stem: Linear search checks the items of an unsorted list one by one until it finds the target. Which describes its best, average and worst case for n items?
options: Best O(1), average O(n), worst O(n)
Best O(1), average O(log n), worst O(n)
Best O(n), average O(n), worst O(n)
Best O(1), average O(1), worst O(n)
questions.explanation: Best case: the target is first, 1 comparison. Worst case: it is last or missing, n comparisons. On average it checks about n/2 items, and n/2 is still O(n): dropping the constant ½ does not make it logarithmic. The loop can stop early, so the best case is not O(n).

questions.stem:
How much extra space does this function use (tightest Big-O)?

```python
def squares(n):
    result = []
    for i in range(n):
        result.append(i * i)
    return result
```
options: O(n), because the list it builds holds n values
O(1), because it only uses two variables, result and i
O(n²), because each stored value is i squared
It depends on how fast the computer is
questions.explanation: Space complexity measures how memory grows with n. `result` ends up holding n numbers, so the extra space is O(n). Counting variable *names* is the trap: one name can refer to a list of n items. Storing i² instead of i does not change how many values are stored, and complexity never depends on the machine.

options: O(n log n), because the inner loop runs fewer than n times
O(n), because the inner loop runs i times, not n times
O(2ⁿ), because the inner loop grows on every pass
O(n²), because it runs 0 + 1 + … + (n − 1) times in total
questions.explanation: The inner loop runs i times, so the total is 0 + 1 + 2 + … + (n − 1) = n(n − 1)/2, about n²/2. Dropping the ½ gives O(n²). A shorter inner loop halves the work but does not change the growth rate; O(n log n) would need the inner loop to run only about log n times.

questions.stem:
What is the time complexity (tightest Big-O) of this code?

```python
for i in range(n):
    j = 1
    while j < n:
        j = j * 2
```
options: O(n²)
O(n log n)
O(n)
O(log n)
questions.explanation: The inner `while` doubles j, so it runs about log₂ n times. It runs once for each of the n outer iterations, giving n × log n. It is not O(n²), because the inner loop jumps 1, 2, 4, 8, ... instead of stepping through every value up to n.

questions.stem: An O(n²) algorithm takes 2 seconds on 1,000 items. Roughly how long should it take on 2,000 items?
options: 4 seconds
8 seconds
6 seconds
16 seconds
questions.explanation: With n² growth, doubling n multiplies the work by 2² = 4, so 2 s × 4 = 8 s. 4 seconds is what a *linear* algorithm would take (double the input, double the time); 16 seconds would be cubic growth (2³ = 8 times as long).

questions.stem: In Python, what does the test `x in items` cost when `items` holds n values?
options: O(1) for both a list and a set
O(n) for a list, O(1) on average for a set
O(log n) for a list, O(1) for a set
O(n) for both a list and a set
questions.explanation: A list has to be scanned item by item until x is found: O(n). A set is a hash table: it computes where x would be stored and looks only there, O(1) on average. A list is not kept sorted, so there is no O(log n) shortcut.

questions.stem: Algorithm A takes 100n steps and algorithm B takes n² steps on an input of size n. Which statement is true?
options: A is faster for every input size, because O(n) beats O(n²)
They are equally fast, because Big-O ignores constants
B is always faster, because 100 is a large constant
B is faster when n < 100, and A is faster when n > 100
questions.explanation: At n = 100 both take 10,000 steps. Below that n² is smaller (n = 50: 2,500 versus 5,000), so B wins; above it n² grows faster (n = 200: 40,000 versus 20,000), so A wins. Big-O says which algorithm wins *for large enough n*, not for every n.
The inner loop runs 4 times for each of the 3 outer iterations: 3 × 4 = 12. Adding (3 + 4 = 7) is the rule for loops one *after* another, not for nested loops.

questions.stem:
What does `steps(64)` return?

```python
def steps(n):
    count = 0
    while n > 1:
        n = n // 2
        count += 1
    return count
```
questions.explanation: 64 → 32 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1 is six halvings, so `count` is 6 = log₂ 64. The loop stops as soon as n is 1, so there is no seventh step. 32 is n/2, the answer you get if you think the loop runs half as many times as n.

O(n²)
O(log n)
questions.explanation: The inner loop always runs exactly 10 times, whatever n is, so `print` runs 10n times: O(n). Nested loops only give O(n²) when *both* loops depend on n.

options: A list with no negative numbers
A list whose first number is negative
A list whose middle number is negative
Every list of 1,000 numbers takes the same time
questions.explanation: The loop returns at the first negative number. With no negatives at all it must check all 1,000 numbers before returning False: the worst case, O(n). A negative first number is the best case, O(1). Inputs of the same size can take very different amounts of work.
